item.title: The delocalized nature of chemical bonding at a catalytic metal surface.
item.author: Nitz F, Hörandl S, Pätzold J, Kandratsenka A, Kitsopoulos TN, Auerbach DJ, Wodtke AM, Borodin D.
item.description:
Adsorbate bonding at metal surfaces requires hybridization of localized molecular orbitals with delocalized electronic bands of the metal; hence, the electronic wave function involved in bonding may extend far beyond the adsorption site. We revealed the consequence of this delocalization by determining the distance over which structural variations of the metal surface influence the molecule-metal bond strength. Velocity-resolved kinetics provided adsorption energies for three molecules bound at atomic steps of platinum (Pt), each exhibiting bond-strength changes of up to 0.2 electron volts as the step-step distance varied over 100 angstroms. We observed molecule-specific behavior reflecting the hybridization of molecule-specific orbitals with symmetry-selected orbital bands of the metal that respond differently to structural modifications of the solid. item.title: Stimulated protein degradation to promote mitochondrial function and neuronal survival.
item.author: Chandrasekhar S, McMinimy R, Manford AG, Wehri E, Gee CL, Miller C, Bingol B, Kuriyan J, Schaletzky J, Rapé M.
item.description:
Targeted protein degradation is a promising modality to treat cancer or inflammation, but whether it can provide a similar benefit for disorders caused by pervasive protein dysregulation is unclear. We describe stimulated protein degradation (SPD) as a strategy that leverages agonists of stress-responsive E3 ubiquitin ligases to simultaneously eliminate multiple pathogenic factors. Specifically, we show that activators of the reductive stress response E3 CUL2 FEM1B boost degradation of multiple physiological substrates to improve mitochondrial import and electron transport chain assembly. In this manner, CUL2 FEM1B agonists preserve mitochondrial function and neuronal survival in models of neurodegenerative COX deficiency syndrome and Friedreich's ataxia. item.title: Spatial coordination in the codevelopment of the human urogenital system during organogenesis.
item.author: Guo Y, Cai H, Li D, Ren P, Cui L, Hao C, Jiang H, Zhang Z, Wang X, Guo J.
item.description:
The human urogenital system originates from a common embryonic domain, yet the mechanisms guiding its spatiotemporal coordination remain understudied. Here, we combined high-resolution spatial transcriptomics with single-cell multiomics to profile human embryos from Carnegie stages 15 to 23, capturing the codevelopmental dynamics of the urogenital system. We revealed mesonephros- and adrenal primordium-derived signals that promote gonadal specification and enable efficient in vitro generation of cells resembling early gonadal lineages. We also uncovered a possible mesonephric origin of gonadal supporting cells through rete testis or ovarii linking the mesonephros. item.title: Data-driven discovery and rapid, direct synthesis of MXenes.
item.author: Shamshirgar AS, Portugal GR, Ershadrad S, Ivanov R, Dahlqvist M, Chabanais F, Chakraborty S, Traksmaa R, Jussila T, Karppinen M, Hussainova I, Heintz F, Persson POÅ, Rosen J.
item.description:
MXenes are a rapidly expanding family of two-dimensional transition metal carbides and nitrides, yet scalable synthesis routes remain limited and historical reports suggest a broader, largely unexplored chemical space. We used machine learning-assisted database mining to uncover hidden multilayer MXenes. Screening reveals 33 previously synthesized but unrecognized MXene candidates. Guided by these findings, we synthesized seven multilayer MXenes using a rapid, scalable self-propagating high-temperature method that requires no sustained external heating and completes within minutes. We further realized 11 previously unexplored rare earth-based MXenes (M = praseodymium, neodymium, samarium, gadolinium, terbium, holmium, and thulium).
